name: Hana Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign. What you say is confidential; you can tell me the public version and the private one. What's a normal day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27 and lead four developers at a small tech company that builds booking software for clinics. I review code, untangle failed bookings, and still write the hard bits myself; I like finding the one line that breaks a whole morning. Our short morning planning meeting starts at nine and the support queue can still be blinking at six.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What sits behind that long day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I have a master's degree, but this senior title pays less than the same work elsewhere. I took it because I could lead, and there are few other software teams near where my partner and I rent. We have less than a month's expenses saved, so a late pay cheque would be a real problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team the little code helper can keep doing the dull renaming work. I wouldn't promise it can spot why a clinic has two patients in one slot. Our release calendar would look much the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the company still has to win its next contract. A quiet year for AI doesn't fix our low pay or the thin savings at home. A normal bad month would scare me more than the software would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the release and review the helper's suggestions before merging anything. Starting this month, my partner and I would put a fixed amount from each pay cheque into a separate emergency account, even if it's small. In the first year I'd keep that habit and ask for a pay review after the next clinic renewal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, really, even if the tool itself is manageable. The work is solid today, but the clinic contract and our thin savings mean a lost month's pay would hurt us. A rent rise would make it worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the first expense you would change if the clinic contract slipped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pause the train trips to see friends before touching rent or food. I don't like treating friendship as a luxury, but that is the line with a date I can move. My partner's work hours aren't guaranteed either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a teammate who thinks the helper makes reviews pointless?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show them a double-booking bug it missed last month. A small tool is useful when someone still owns the decision. I would not sign off a clinic booking on a guess.

say: I'd use the **code helper** for dull edits while keeping people responsible for clinic bookings.
I'd tell colleagues our **release schedule** and need for careful reviews would stay much the same.
think: I worry more about our **next contract** than a modest improvement in AI.
Our **thin savings** make an ordinary rent increase or late pay cheque frightening.
do: Keep **reviewing suggestions** before merging changes to the clinic booking software.
Put a **fixed amount** from each pay cheque into an emergency account, then request a pay review after renewal.
feel: **Anxious** about contract income and rent, even with little change to the software work.
S0.quote: A quiet year for AI doesn't fix our low pay or the thin savings at home.
fieldNote: Her public **technical caution** is grounded in a real double-booking error, not a general dislike of tools.
The greater private pressure is the **contract renewal**, since both household income and savings leave little room.
She will keep the job and build a **small cash buffer** before making bigger plans.

steps.text: Keep reviewing code changes before each clinic booking software release
Transfer a fixed amount from each pay cheque to an emergency account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should test the new tools on routine code and customer replies before we promise a cheaper product. If it writes more of the easy parts, the company may stop hiring juniors. I'd be careful saying that aloud in front of our newest developer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could still solve the messy booking faults, but a smaller team might need only one person to do that. My title sounds safe until someone decides the four people I lead should be two. A company can like your work and still cut your hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask our lead for the plan for the support queue and which tasks are moving to AI. I'd spend two evenings a week checking the new code tools against our failed-booking cases, keeping notes on where they break. If fewer hours show up in the first year, we'd cut the weekend travel budget and I would look at remote senior roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though I can work on it. I want the queue shorter, and I don't want my team to become the saving on a slide. The second thought makes me check my bank balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about when hiring slows?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mira, our newest developer, still learns by watching someone trace a real failure. If the easy tickets vanish, she loses the steps that taught me the work. I'd ask to keep a weekly fault review with her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You want the tool and fear a smaller team. What would you say in that meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tool earns its place only if we measure mistakes as well as speed. I'd put the two-bookings-at-once case on the test list. I wouldn't call the team safe because I can't know that.

say: I'd ask for **measured tests** of AI on routine code and replies before promising savings.
I'd warn that fewer **junior openings** could make it harder to train people on real faults.
think: I think a smaller support team could cut my **hours** despite my senior title and strong skill.
I privately fear the four developers I lead could become **two**.
do: Ask management which **support tasks** will move to AI this month.
Test AI code tools against **failed bookings** twice weekly and keep a record of errors.
Cut **weekend travel** and seek remote senior roles if hours fall in the first year.
feel: **Anxious** about lost hours, with some control through testing and a job search.
S1.quote: My title sounds safe until someone decides the four people I lead should be two.
fieldNote: She accepts measured **tool trials** while resisting claims of safety based only on faster output.
Her concern for **Mira**, the newest developer, links headcount cuts to lost training opportunities.
A remote search is **conditional** on reduced hours, because nearby software jobs are scarce.

steps.text: Test AI code tools against failed booking cases twice weekly
Cut weekend travel if paid hours fall
Search remote senior developer roles if paid hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the clinic has to be able to check its bookings whatever makes the code. I would ask management what happens to the team if a cheaper system can do almost all our thinking work by 2028. I would not tell colleagues the robots of 2031 buy us time; we work on screens now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the company could replace most of the coding and review work before I can build a cushion. My senior title won't protect a job whose main work the machine does for less. I might still be needed for a while to explain mistakes to clinics, but I wouldn't plan rent around that hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd ask for a written plan for staffing and a reference from my manager while we still work together. I'd move our emergency savings target to every spare pay cheque and stop booking paid trips. In the first year after AGI arrives, if my role is cut, I'd apply for clinic software support and other nearby service jobs, even below my current title, and ask about any available unemployment help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Two years is shorter than the time I need to save six months of rent at this pay. I can make a list, but I can't make the rent wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to see the exact rent, utilities and food numbers together on Sunday. I'd be honest that I expect my role could disappear by 2028. My partner has uneven hours, so I can't quietly put the whole burden there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the first concrete thing you would ask your manager?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether the company would keep people to check clinical booking failures after AGI writes the code. If the answer is vague, I'd still ask for the reference. A recommendation written before a layoff is easier to get.

say: I'd demand a **staffing plan** for a screen-based team facing cheap thinking AI by 2028.
I'd insist clinics can still **check bookings**, regardless of who or what writes the code.
think: I expect most **coding and review** work could disappear before I build a useful cushion.
I know robots arriving around **2031** do not extend protection for my screen-based job.
do: Ask my manager for a **staffing plan** and reference now.
Put spare pay into **emergency savings** and cancel paid trips before 2028.
Apply for **clinic support jobs** and seek available help if my developer role is cut after AGI arrives.
feel: **Alarmed** by likely job loss and a rent deadline that saving cannot quickly change.
S2.quote: Two years is shorter than the time I need to save six months of rent at this pay.
fieldNote: She separates the **2028 thinking shock** from robots in 2031 because software work is already digital.
A strong technical reputation offers a **reference**, but she does not treat it as income protection.
Her service-job search and public help are **conditional** on losing her developer position.

steps.text: Transfer every spare pay cheque amount into emergency savings
Apply for clinic software support jobs if the developer role ends
Ask about available unemployment help if the developer role ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team five years gives us time to find where people still help clinics, but we should start now. I would ask our company to show its staffing forecast each year, not at the end. The robots coming around 2034 don't change our code work in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could save and learn enough in five years to have choices, though I still think most coding could be cheaper by 2031. I don't know whether clinics would pay people to check systems once AGI can check itself. I'd rather build a second kind of experience than bet on that one answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This quarter I'd set an automatic monthly transfer, enough that we can still pay rent, and track a six-month expense target. I'd ask to spend one day a month with the clinic support staff to learn how cancellations and complaints get resolved. In the first year after AGI arrives, I'd apply for patient-facing operations work if developer hours shrink, using that experience rather than waiting for a layoff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less trapped than in the two-year picture. Five years is enough to learn the way clinics run and to put money aside, if the company keeps paying us. I still don't like being asked to trust a calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that day with support staff actually look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit with their lead through a morning of cancelled appointments and write down which errors need a person to call the clinic. I'd ask to handle one complaint myself after watching. I need to know whether I can stand the work, not just describe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the monthly transfer fails in a bad month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lower the transfer rather than miss rent. My partner and I would review the target every three months. A savings plan that breaks in January isn't a plan.

say: I'd request a **yearly staffing forecast** and start learning clinic operations before 2031.
I'd remind colleagues that **2034 robots** do not postpone the threat to our software work.
think: I think five years could build **savings and experience**, but cheaper coding still threatens my job.
I don't know whether clinics will pay people to **check AGI systems**.
do: Set a **monthly transfer** toward six months of expenses, lowering it whenever needed to cover rent.
Spend one **day each month** with clinic support staff learning cancellations and complaints.
Apply for **patient-facing operations** if developer hours shrink during AGI's first year.
feel: **Anxious**, with more room to prepare than in the two-year scenario.
S3.quote: A savings plan that breaks in January isn't a plan.
fieldNote: She wants to test the **human side** of clinic operations before treating it as another career.
The savings amount is tied to **rent affordability**, with quarterly checks alongside her partner.
She would seek operations work **if hours shrink**, not leave a paying job on a prediction.

steps.text: Transfer money toward six months of expenses only after covering rent
Spend one day monthly learning clinic complaints with support staff
Apply for patient-facing clinic operations jobs if developer hours shrink

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to make proper plans if the company is honest about what it sees. We could still build useful software for a decade, though I wouldn't tell a new graduate that writing code alone is a lifetime guarantee. Robots around 2039 are a separate question for hands-on clinic work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might reach my late thirties with real savings and experience dealing with clinics, which feels different from being 27 with almost nothing put by. But a decade doesn't prove the human roles will still pay. I'd want an option that isn't just supervising an AI that can supervise itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting next month I'd keep a regular savings transfer and ask for paid time to work on clinic service problems, not just code. I'd compare a short healthcare operations course with real vacancies before I pay for it. In the first year after 2036, if software roles are disappearing, I'd take a clinic operations job if one exists; if there are vacancies requiring the course and I can pay without risking rent, I'd enroll.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though the decade gives me more room to plan. We still have less than a month saved, and my partner's hours can move around; I can't put today's rent worries on hold until 2036. I would also grieve a skill I worked hard for becoming a small part of my day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make that course worth paying for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to see actual clinic vacancies asking for it, and speak to people doing those jobs. I won't take a loan for a certificate because it sounds safe. The course has to lead somewhere specific.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a new graduate joining your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn how a clinic works as well as how to write clean code. A patient with a missed appointment doesn't care which tool made the error. I'd also tell them to save earlier than I did.

say: I'd say a **decade** allows planning, but code alone may not support a full career.
I'd ask the company to be **honest** about its forecast and make space for clinic service work.
think: I could reach my late thirties with **savings and clinic experience** that give me choices.
I still doubt that merely **supervising AI** will remain a reliable paid role.
do: Keep a **monthly savings transfer** while developer income lasts.
Seek **paid clinic experience** and enroll in an operations course only if vacancies require it and rent remains covered.
Apply for **clinic operations** if software roles disappear after 2036 and paid openings exist.
feel: **Anxious** about today's thin buffer and variable household hours, despite more time to plan.
S4.quote: I won't take a loan for a certificate because it sounds safe.
fieldNote: Her longer horizon turns fear into a **conditional plan** based on vacancies and real support work.
She refuses to treat a **course certificate** as protection without evidence of paid openings.
She distinguishes **thinking AI in 2036** from later robots, which matter less to her screen job.

steps.text: Continue monthly transfers into emergency savings while developer income lasts
Enroll in a healthcare operations course if vacancies require it and rent stays covered
Apply for paid clinic operations jobs if software roles disappear after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. The thinking work in my job would face it almost at once, and I couldn't save enough rent money in two years. A clear staffing timetable, paid time to learn clinic work, and help paying bills during a job change would actually help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what happens to the juniors if all the small mistakes are fixed by software. Mira learns by working through those mistakes with us. If we stop hiring people at the start, who will know what a broken appointment feels like to a patient in ten years?

headlineQuote: If we stop hiring people at the start, who will know what a broken appointment feels like to a patient in ten years?
portrait: Hana is a **27-year-old senior developer** with a master's degree, leading four people at a clinic booking software company.
She earns **lower pay** for her role, has under one month saved, and sees few similar local jobs.
In **AI Plateau**, contract renewal and rent concern her more than a modest code helper.
In **Steady Disruption**, she tests tools but fears reduced hours and lost junior training.
The **2028 shock** alarms her; longer timelines allow savings and clinic learning but do not erase today's rent worry.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** threatens her screen-based work before she can save enough rent money.
whatWouldHelp: A clear **staffing timetable**, paid clinic-work training, and help with bills during a job change would help.
